items.abstract_or_text: Stanford discovered something equivalent to “Dopamine Neurons” inside LLMs They call it "Sparse Reward Subsystem". Biological brains use a specialized reward subsystem to learn, adapt, and survive. Now, researchers have proven that large language models built the exact same thing inside their hidden states by accident.

items.abstract_or_text: GPT-6 Astra has set a new ECI record, with a score of 169. This is a substantial jump from the prior best (163), but is within our uncertainty range for the reasoning-era ECI trend. Astra also set new records on our math, continual learning, and game-puzzles benchmarks. On our long-horizon coding benchmark, MirrorCode, Astra ranks between Opus 4.7 and Fable 5. OpenAI gave us pre-release access to test Astra. Charts and more details for Astra’s individual benchmark results in the thread.

items.title: @rohanpaul_ai：Society's cognitive dependence on AI. A massive paper from Harvard and many other top universities. A small increase in
items.abstract_or_text: Society's cognitive dependence on AI. A massive paper from Harvard and many other top universities. A small increase in LLM adoption could trigger a much larger jump in cognitive dependence on AI, so the paper argues we should protect independent reasoning before that tipping point. The paper treats AI dependence as a feedback problem. As more people hand reading, writing, reasoning, or verification to LLMs, the habits that keep those skills active can weaken too. That creates a possible tipping point. Adoption can rise gradually, then suddenly settle into a state where much more thinking is outsourced. Once that happens, simply reducing AI use may not restore the old level of independence.

items.title: @HowToPrompt__：MIT and Harvard published a paper with a devastating title: "The Coasean Singularity" They mathematically proved that AI
items.abstract_or_text: MIT and Harvard published a paper with a devastating title: "The Coasean Singularity" They mathematically proved that AI will destroy the economy. For decades, economics has relied on a foundational rule laid out in 1937 by Ronald Coase: Why do companies even exist? His answer was transaction costs. Finding prices, negotiating contracts, verifying identities, and managing logistics are hard, expensive, and messy. That friction is why we build corporations, to bring people under one roof so we don't have to contract out every single task. Now, AI agents are destroying that friction. The researchers mapped out what happens when autonomous software can search, negotiate, verify, and execute contracts at near-zero marginal cost. When transaction costs drop to zero, the entire purpose of a traditional company evaporates. That’s the Coasean Singularity.

No single record understands real work, because real work touches all systems a company runs on. Do the whole job better than anyone and you unlock a learning loop that compounds.
